one_liner: Book example: std::stack behind a test-and-test-and-set spinlock, about 2.3x the single-thread push/pop rate of a std::mutex-guarded stack.
what_it_does: Chapter07/02_stack.C wraps std::stack<T> (std::deque underneath) in mt_stack, whose push(), pop() and top() each take a std::lock_guard on the hand-written spinlock from Chapter07/spinlock.h, and benchmarks it against mt_stack1, the identical wrapper on std::mutex. pop() and top() return std::optional<T>, empty when the stack is empty, so callers never race between an empty() check and a pop. The same header also defines rw_spinlock, a reader-writer spinlock used by rw_stack. It is teaching code of about 25 lines for the lock plus the wrapper, not a library.
how_it_is_fast: The lock is test-and-test-and-set: a waiter spins on a relaxed load and only tries exchange(1, acquire) when the flag reads free, and unlock() is a single release store. After every 8 failed attempts the waiter calls nanosleep for 1 ns as backoff. Uncontended, lock and unlock are inline atomic operations on a 4-byte flag, while std::mutex lock/unlock go through the platform threads library; the single-thread benchmark measures exactly this uncontended path, not behaviour under contention.
when_to_use: Very short critical sections, such as a push or pop of a small value, where the lock is mostly uncontended and the lock/unlock cost itself dominates.
Low thread counts on dedicated or pinned cores, where a lock holder is rarely preempted while others spin.
Linux or other POSIX targets on x86-64 (the header calls POSIX nanosleep; the book's figures come from an x86 machine).
As the coarse-locked baseline before trying a lock-free stack: the record notes the same chapter finds the lock-free stack does not beat this spinlock stack on x86.
when_not_to_use: Oversubscribed or loaded machines, or threads that can be preempted while holding the lock: waiters burn CPU, there is no fairness or priority inheritance, and one thread can starve.

Latency-sensitive waiters: after 8 failed spins a waiter sleeps in nanosleep, and on Linux the requested 1 ns is stretched by the thread's timer slack (50 microseconds for init and inherited by default, per the PR_SET_TIMERSLACK man page seen via a search snippet; not applied to real-time scheduling policies), so a contended acquire can take tens of microseconds.

Code that needs try_lock, timed locking, recursion or blocking waits: spinlock has only lock() and unlock(), so it cannot go into std::scoped_lock with several locks or std::try_lock, and std::condition_variable needs std::mutex (std::condition_variable_any would be required).

Windows/MSVC: spinlock.h uses POSIX nanosleep, 02_stack.C uses unistd.h sysconf, and rw_spinlock's 0x1000000000000000L constant needs a 64-bit long, which Windows' 32-bit long is not, although the top-level README lists Visual Studio and Windows.
Message passing between threads: the sibling queues (atomic_queue, moodycamel, Boost.Lockfree) are built for it, while this is a LIFO with one coarse lock.

integration.dependencies: none for spinlock.h beyond POSIX nanosleep; the benchmark needs Google Benchmark 1.5.x (it reads state.thread_index and state.threads as data members)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (class template argument deduction in std::lock_guard g(l_), std::optional); compiler and flags for the book figures not documented
integration.thread_safety: push, pop and top lock; reset() does not, and the benchmark calls it from thread 0 before the timed loop
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — mt_stack has the same interface as the std::mutex version mt_stack1, and spinlock meets BasicLockable for std::lock_guard and std::unique_lock, but without try_lock it cannot replace std::mutex in std::scoped_lock of several locks, std::try_lock or std::condition_variable

gotchas: 02_stack.C does not compile against Google Benchmark 1.6.0 or later: it uses state.thread_index and state.threads as data members, which 1.6.0 turned into the member functions thread_index() and threads() (1.5.6 still has the fields).

The spin loop has no CPU pause instruction, and the 4-byte flag has no alignas padding, so it can share a cache line with the std::stack's own fields or neighbouring globals; both matter under contention, not in the single-thread figure.

One benchmark item is a push plus a pop (Arg(1)), counted the same on both sides. In multi-thread runs a pop that finds the stack empty still counts, and items per second are summed over threads with real time, so an unfair lock that lets one thread run while the others sleep can post high aggregate throughput; per-thread latency and fairness are not reported.
ThreadRange(1, numcpu) takes numcpu from sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_CONF), which counts configured CPUs (offline ones included), so the top thread count can exceed the CPUs actually online.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: If you want to keep a std::stack or std::queue and only swap the lock, this 25-line spinlock and eventpp::SpinLock are the same idea; eventpp's is packaged in a maintained library with its own benchmark (about 1.4x over std::mutex), this one is easier to read and copy. For cross-thread queues, atomic_queue, moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue or Boost.Lockfree avoid the lock entirely and report several-fold lower latency than std::mutex; prefer this only for LIFO order with tiny, mostly uncontended critical sections.
verified_claims_summary: The book, relayed by the seed lead and not present in the repo, reports about 70 million push/pop pairs per second for the spinlock stack against about 30 million for the std::mutex stack on one thread of an unnamed x86 machine (about 2.3x, derived), with an unlocked std::stack at about 485 million; compiler, flags, standard library and CPU model are not given. The checked-in Google Benchmark harness (02_stack.C, Arg(1), real time) runs exactly this comparison, but its single-thread point measures only uncontended lock cost.
